title: Should School Start Later?
subject: English language arts
instructions: Read the op-ed, then answer. Write your ID number, not your name.

questions.title: Let Teenagers Sleep
questions.text:
Every weekday at 6:15 a.m., thousands of teenagers in our district drag themselves out of bed for a 7:30 first bell. We tell them to try harder, go to bed earlier, put the phone away. But the problem isn't willpower. During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts later by as much as two hours, so a sixteen-year-old who falls asleep at 11 p.m. is doing what biology tells her to do.

When a district in Seattle moved its high school start time from 7:50 to 8:45, students slept a median of 34 minutes more each night, and their grades in a required biology course rose. At one of the two schools, attendance improved too. Critics say later start times wreck sports schedules and bus routes. Those are real costs. But they are problems of logistics, and logistics can be solved. Sleep cannot be made up on Saturday.
questions.source: An original op-ed written for this worksheet; the Seattle figures come from a 2018 University of Washington study.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best states the author's claim?

options.text: Teenagers should put their phones away so they fall asleep earlier.
options.why: The author rejects that fix: the problem isn't willpower.

options.text: High schools should start later because teenagers' sleep needs are biological.
options.why: Yes: every paragraph builds toward a later start.

options.text: Sports schedules and bus routes matter more than an hour of sleep.
options.why: The author calls those costs real but solvable.

options.text: Seattle's later start time raised students' biology grades.
options.why: That's evidence the author uses, not the claim.

questions.prompt: Counterargument: The author admits later start times have 'real costs.' Write a paragraph that evaluates how well the author answers this counterargument. Cite at least two lines.

rubric.criterion: Claim: takes a clear position on how well the author answers the counterargument.
levels: a clear position that weighs what the author does well and what's missing

rubric.criterion: Evidence: quotes or cites specific lines (e.g. 'those are problems of logistics' or the Seattle results) accurately.
Reasoning: explains how the evidence supports the position, not just restating it.
Conventions: sentences are complete and readable; errors don't get in the way of meaning.
